Graft donor site healing

Several palatal donor-site trials found faster early epithelialization or better healing scores, but pain results were mixed. In a small skin-graft donor-site series, pain decreased without measurable improvement in wound closure, area, or quality.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Several palatal donor-site trials found faster early epithelialization or better healing scores, but pain results were mixed. In a small skin-graft donor-site series, pain decreased without measurable improvement in wound closure, area, or quality.

Summary of the Evidence

Twenty-one relevant publications were identified: 17 empirical human reports, two animal publications, and two systematic reviews that overlap the primary studies. Most human reports concern palatal wounds after free-gingival grafting; others examine skin-graft or burn-graft donor sites. A donor-site record on hematoma beneath grafted skin and a water-filtered infrared-A infection case were excluded because they do not directly test PBM for donor-wound healing. These distinct wound types should not be treated as one uniform clinical outcome.

Human and clinical evidence

Several randomized studies of palatal donor sites reported faster early epithelialization. In a 40-person trial, complete epithelialization was more common by day 14, bleeding was lower during the first two days, and healing scores were higher after laser treatment (Ustaoglu et al. 2017). A 2025 trial of 30 people found more donor sites with complete epithelial coverage by day 10, but no significant difference in overall wound closure, pain, or analgesic use (Paz et al. 2025). Another trial found quicker donor-site epithelialization but no pain difference, showing that healing and discomfort do not always move together (Sargolzaei et al. 2025).

For skin-graft donor sites, a controlled 21-person case series found lower pain on day five but no difference in re-epithelialization time, wound area, or wound-quality scores (Carboni et al. 2021). These results support a possible pain effect in that sample, not faster skin-wound closure.

Animal evidence

Two animal publications examined donor wounds. A rat study reported faster palatal repair after 660-nm red LED exposure. In a rabbit skin-wound experiment, epithelialization time and contraction did not significantly differ from controls, although tissue vascularity changed. The same publication found some human-fibroblast growth values increased in culture, but not significantly.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate laboratory programme was identified. The fibroblast work was part of the rabbit-wound publication, so it is not an independent line of clinical evidence.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols include 660-nm red visible LEDs, 940–970-nm near-infrared diode lasers, and some 808-nm near-infrared treatment. One 940-nm trial used 5 J/cm² over 30 seconds for 11 sessions; a 660-nm skin-donor protocol used 1.53 J/cm² for 600 seconds on five postoperative days. Other reports incompletely specify dose. Sites, comparators, schedules, and healing measures vary, and no trial establishes one best protocol.

Interpretation

The most repeated favorable human result is faster early epithelialization at palatal donor sites. Pain relief is less consistent, and skin-donor studies do not show the same objective closure result. The interpretation therefore depends on the donor site and on whether the outcome is closure, tissue quality, bleeding, or pain.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low to moderate for faster early epithelialization at palatal donor sites.

Low for pain reduction across oral and skin donor sites.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Several controlled palatal-graft studies report faster early epithelialization, while other trials found no difference in overall closure or pain. In skin-graft donor sites, one small controlled series reduced pain without improving measured healing. Because results vary by site and outcome, larger trials using consistent healing and pain measures would be needed to support a stronger rating.
